title: What If a Nuclear Reactor Fell From Orbit? In 1978 One Hit Canada

scenes.text: What if a nuclear reactor fell out of orbit? In 1978, one did. Canada sent a bill.
Kosmos 954 was a Soviet spy satellite that tracked ships by radar, powered by a reactor holding about 50 kilograms of uranium.
At the end of its life, the core was meant to be boosted into a safe, high orbit. The system failed.
On January 24, 1978, it burned up over northern Canada and scattered radioactive debris along a 600-kilometer track.
Canadian and American teams searched 124,000 square kilometers of frozen wilderness for months. One fragment was radioactive enough to kill within hours.
Most of the fuel was never found. Canada billed the Soviet Union six million dollars. It paid three.

description:
What if a nuclear reactor fell out of orbit?
One did. Kosmos 954 was a Soviet radar ocean-reconnaissance satellite launched on 18 September 1977 and powered by a small reactor containing about 50 kg of highly enriched uranium. When it began to fail, the system meant to boost the reactor core into a safe disposal orbit did not work, and on 24 January 1978 the satellite re-entered over Canada's Northwest Territories, scattering radioactive debris along a track of about 600 km from Great Slave Lake towards Baker Lake. In Operation Morning Light, Canadian and American teams searched about 124,000 square kilometres until October 1978. They recovered a dozen large pieces and thousands of small particles, including one fragment radioactive enough to be lethal within a few hours of contact, but only a tiny fraction of the fuel. Canada billed the Soviet Union C$6,041,174.70 under the 1972 space liability convention; the USSR eventually paid C$3 million.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: The exact bill was 6,041,174 dollars and 70 cents. What else do you think is still up there waiting to come down?
